GenAlpha Brings a Practical Approach for Analog AI to DAC 2026by Mike Gianfagna on 08-31-2026 at 10:00 am

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: AI, EDA, Events, GenAIpha

Key takeaways ▼

Agentic AI was everywhere at DAC 2026. Various focus areas were presented that covered many parts of the chip design flow. Verification and debug were a popular topic since so much time is spent there. Analog design is another pressure point. Every chip design has analog content. While the size of the analog blocks may not be huge, the design task for the analog part can take 100X longer than the rest of the chip, creating the possibility of a critical bottleneck.
Analog design is a highly complex process, so adding AI has some unique challenges. There were a few companies who focused on this area at DAC. The approach that one of those companies proposed caught my attention. It was based on years of doing analog design and analyzing how to make it better. I’m a fan of “automate, then optimize”, so I wanted to learn more. Here is what I found as GenAlpha brings a practical approach for analog AI to DAC 2026.
My Conversation with the Founder and CEO
Dr. Dan Fritchman
I was fortunate to be able to spend some time with Dan Fritchman, founder and CEO of GenAlpha. Dan is both an electrical engineer and semiconductor-software entrepreneur.
He spent about 10 years at Apple, working on the analog and mixed-signal portions of iPhone and iPad SoCs. During that time, he developed an appreciation for the truly creative and challenging work associated with analog design. He also got a first-hand perspective on the “turn the crank” part of the process, where ideas were explored and there never seemed to be enough time to converge on the best answer.
This experience was the inspiration for Dan to form GenAlpha. He earned his Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences at UC Berkeley in 2023. His dissertation, An Integrated Circuit Design Framework for Human, Computer, and ML Designers, focused on software infrastructure that allows people, conventional programs, and machine-learning systems to collaborate on chip design.
GenAlpha grew out of a focus on applying modern software and AI techniques to make analog and other complex chip-design processes faster and less dependent on repetitive manual engineering work. The company joined Berkeley SkyDeck’s 2024 incubator cohort. The first areas of focus for GenAlpha was analog layout.
Dan focused on the very human relationship between a circuit designer and the layout designer working on the project. Initially there is a very high level of interaction between the circuit designer and the layout designer. “Try this. No, move that. Resize that part see what happens…”
Dan explained he coordinated a lot of those processes. I spent a fair amount of time in analog design as well; I was part of those same discussions. It should also be mentioned that there is never enough analog layout designers. Getting time with one can be a difficult and frustrating experience.
What GenAlpha provides are AI agents to perform layout design. These agents can work at various levels of autonomy to match the needs of the circuit designer. The speed and accuracy of the AI agents allow the circuit designer to cover a lot more ground than the old fully manual process. Trying more options finds a better design, and the level of interaction between the human and the AI can change as the human gets more confident in the AI.
There is still a lot of detailed information to balance with these tasks, but the model of gradually increasing automation to match the needs of the circuit designer seems to work quite well. This is the practical approach I mentioned in the title of the post. That is, focus on the current process of analog layout and make it more efficient by introducing AI to blend into the process. The skills the analog agents deliver is substantial. Dan is very well versed in the processes involved and ensuring the AI agents have the appropriate depth to navigate the complexities of analog design is a key area of focus for the company.
Dan explained that the current focus is analog layout. That will then expand to analog circuit design and then mixed-signal design. Given the practical, well-grounded approach taken by GenAlpha I can’t wait to see how the roadmap fills out. Analog design clearly needs a lot of help, and GenAlpha is well positioned to make a significant impact.
